title: Real‑World Combo: Substitution + Arrays 🔗
description: Store command output directly into arrays, build dynamic menus, and process file lists.

slides.title: Loading Command Output into an Array 📥
slides.content:
## The Missing Map

You can't directly `arr=$(ls)`. Instead, use `mapfile` (or `readarray`) to read lines into an array:

```bash
mapfile -t lines < <(ls)
```
- `-t` strips trailing newlines.
- `< <(command)` is process substitution that feeds the command's output as a file.

Older method: `IFS=$'\n' read -r -a arr < <(command)`, but `mapfile` is cleaner.

slides.title: Read Files into Array
slides.codeSnippet:
mapfile -t txt_files < <(find . -name "*.txt")
for f in "${txt_files[@]}"; do echo "$f"; done

quizData.question: What does `mapfile -t arr < <(command)` do?

options.text: Runs the command and stores its exit code in arr
Reads each line of the command output into an array element
Maps the command's arguments to an array

quizData.explanation: `mapfile` (or `readarray`) reads lines from stdin into an indexed array; `-t` removes the newline from each line.

slides.title: Building a Dynamic Menu with Arrays 🖥️
slides.content:
## Select from a List

Use an array to hold menu options and a loop to display them. Combine `select` (built‑in) or manual numbering.

```bash
options=("Show date" "List files" "Exit")
select opt in "${options[@]}"; do
   case $opt in ...) ... ;; esac
done
```
`select` automatically numbers the options.

slides.title: Select Menu
slides.content: Create a simple interactive menu using an array:

quizData.question: `select var in "${arr[@]}"` uses the elements of the array as menu options.
quizData.explanation: Yes, `select` iterates over the provided list and presents them as numbered choices.

slides.title: Reading Configuration into an Associative Array ⚙️
slides.content:
## Parse key=value Pairs

A common pattern: load a config file into an associative array.
```bash
declare -A config
while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
   config[$key]=$value
done < config.ini
```
Skip comments and blank lines with `grep -v '^#'`.

slides.title: Config Loader
slides.codeSnippet:
declare -A settings
while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
  settings[$key]=$value
done <<< "user=admin
port=8080"
echo "User: ${settings[user]}, Port: ${settings[port]}"

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `printf '%s\n' "${arr[@]}"` to print each array element on its own line – handy for piping to other tools.
